title: Stage 8 Science — Practice Test 1
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Practice test
summary: A full, timed end-of-Stage-8 science practice test in Cambridge style: two 45-minute papers of 50 marks each, covering biology, chemistry, physics, Earth and space and investigation skills, with a mark scheme and worked solution for every question.

items: This is a full practice end-of-Stage-8 science test written in the style of Cambridge Lower Secondary. The Cambridge Lower Secondary Checkpoint itself is taken at the end of Stage 9; this test checks the Stage 8 work that Checkpoint builds on.

There are **two papers**: Paper 1 and Paper 2. Each paper lasts **45 minutes** and is worth **50 marks** (100 marks in total). Both papers mix biology, chemistry, physics, Earth and space, and thinking and working scientifically.

**Calculator:** Paper 1 allows a calculator, as the Cambridge Checkpoint Paper 1 cover says "You may use a calculator". Cambridge has not published the calculator rule for Paper 2, so check with your teacher; every calculation here can be done with careful working.
**Equipment:** a black or dark blue pen, an HB pencil for diagrams and graphs, a ruler and an eraser. No other materials are needed.

Answer **all** questions. The number of marks for each part is shown in brackets [ ]. In questions that say "Show your working", write every step: you can earn a mark for correct working even if the final answer is wrong.
You may write your answers on paper first if you like. You can also download and print the question paper and do the whole test on paper.

How marking works here: typed answers (numbers, single words and multiple choice) are checked automatically. Written answers (explain, describe, suggest) are marked by you, using the mark scheme shown at the end. Be strict with yourself, just as a real examiner would be.
Your score is a practice score to help you prepare. It is not an official Cambridge result.

questions.ms: 1 mark: the two muscles have opposite effects / when one contracts the other relaxes (e.g. A straightens the leg, B bends it). 1 mark: a muscle can only pull (contract); it cannot push, so a second muscle is needed to move the bone back. Do not accept: 'muscles push the bones'.
questions.e: A muscle can only **pull** when it contracts; it cannot push. So one muscle (A) pulls the lower leg straight and another muscle (B) is needed to pull it back to bend the knee. When one contracts, the other relaxes. Two muscles that work against each other like this are an antagonistic pair.

questions.q: (b) Which describes what happens when Youssef breathes in?
c: The diaphragm relaxes and moves up; the ribs move down and in.
The diaphragm contracts and moves down; the ribs move up and out.
The diaphragm contracts and moves up; the ribs move down and in.

questions.e: Breathing in: the diaphragm **contracts and flattens (moves down)** and the intercostal muscles contract to pull the ribs **up and out**. The chest gets bigger, the pressure inside falls and air rushes in. The answer is B.

questions.e: Running muscles need a lot of energy. The energy is released by **aerobic respiration**, which uses oxygen and makes carbon dioxide. So Youssef breathes faster to take in more oxygen for his muscles and to get rid of the extra carbon dioxide.

questions.q: (f) Describe how oxygen gets from the air in the alveoli into Youssef's blood.
questions.ms: 1 mark: by diffusion. 1 mark: from a high concentration (of oxygen) in the alveoli to a low concentration in the blood / through the thin walls of the alveoli and capillaries (one cell thick). Do not accept 'oxygen is pumped' or 'sucked'.
questions.e: Oxygen moves by **diffusion**. There is a high concentration of oxygen in the air in the alveoli and a low concentration in the blood arriving at the lungs, so oxygen moves across the very thin walls of the alveoli and the capillaries into the blood.

Question 3
Egypt has built a very large solar park in the desert near Aswan. Egypt also gets electricity from wind farms and from power stations that burn natural gas.
questions.q: (a) Which list contains **only** renewable energy resources?
c: wind, solar, natural gas
tidal, coal, wind
solar, wind, tidal
oil, natural gas, coal
questions.e: Solar, wind and tidal power will not run out, so they are renewable. Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels, which are non-renewable. The answer is C.

Question 3
Egypt has built a very large solar park in the desert near Aswan. Egypt also gets electricity from wind farms and from power stations that burn natural gas.
questions.q: (b) Suggest **one** reason why the desert in southern Egypt is a good place for a solar park.
questions.ms: 1 mark for any one: a lot of sunshine / many sunny days / clear skies with little cloud / strong sunlight; large areas of empty land that are not used for farming or homes. Do not accept 'it is hot' on its own.
questions.e: Solar panels need sunlight. Southern Egypt has strong sunshine on almost every day of the year, with very few clouds. There is also a lot of empty desert land, so the panels do not take land needed for farms or towns.

questions.q: (c) A company now makes water bottles from bioplastic instead of plastic made from crude oil. Which is an advantage of bioplastic?
c: It is made from plants, which can be grown again, so it is renewable.
It is made from coal, so it lasts for millions of years.
It is made from crude oil, so it is cheaper.
It can never break down, so it does not need recycling.
questions.e: Bioplastics are made from plant materials (for example starch from maize or sugar cane). The plants can be grown again every year, so bioplastic is a **renewable** resource, while crude oil will run out. The answer is A.

questions.q: (d) Explain what holds the electrons in an atom.
questions.ms: 1 mark: electrostatic attraction / the attraction between opposite charges. 1 mark: between the negative electrons and the positive nucleus / positive protons. Do not accept 'gravity' or 'magnetism'.
questions.e: The electrons are negative and the protons in the nucleus are positive. Opposite charges attract, so there is an **electrostatic attraction** between the electrons and the nucleus. This force holds the atom together.

questions.ms: 1 mark for any one: the rat competes with the jerboas for the same food (seeds / grass / plants); it competes for space / burrows / shelter; it brings a new disease that the jerboas cannot fight. The answer must include a reason, not just 'jerboas die'.
questions.e: The rat eats the same food as the jerboa (seeds and grass). It breeds quickly, so it can eat most of the food and the jerboas cannot get enough. This **competition** makes the number of jerboas fall.

Question 7
Athletes need a healthy diet and healthy blood and lungs.
questions.q: (a) Which row shows a good source of vitamin C and one of its functions?
c: fish oil — helps the body take in calcium for strong bones
carrots — needed for good eyesight in dim light
red meat — needed to make haemoglobin in red blood cells
oranges and guava — keep the skin and gums healthy
questions.e: Citrus fruits and guava are rich in **vitamin C**, which keeps skin and gums healthy and helps wounds heal. A describes vitamin D, B vitamin A and C the mineral iron. The answer is D.

questions.p:
Question 7
Athletes need a healthy diet and healthy blood and lungs.
questions.q: (b) The night before a long race, Karim eats a big plate of pasta. Pasta is rich in one nutrient that the body uses mainly as a source of energy. Name this nutrient.
questions.e: Pasta is rich in **carbohydrate** (starch). Carbohydrates are broken down to glucose, which is used in respiration to release energy; extra can be stored for the race.

questions.p:
Question 7
Athletes need a healthy diet and healthy blood and lungs.
questions.q: (c) Name the part of the blood that carries glucose from the small intestine to the muscles.
questions.e: Dissolved nutrients such as glucose, and carbon dioxide, are carried in the **plasma**, the liquid part of the blood.

questions.p:
Question 7
Athletes need a healthy diet and healthy blood and lungs.
questions.q: (d) Explain why a person who smokes usually cannot run as far as a person who does not smoke.
questions.ms: 1 mark for any one cause: carbon monoxide (in smoke) is carried by red blood cells instead of oxygen / reduces the oxygen the blood carries; OR tar / smoke damages the alveoli, so less gas exchange; OR smoke damages the airways / makes mucus. 1 mark: so less oxygen reaches the muscles, so less (aerobic) respiration / less energy is released.
questions.e: Cigarette smoke contains **carbon monoxide**, which is carried by red blood cells in place of oxygen, and tar, which damages the alveoli so less gas exchange happens. Less oxygen reaches the muscles, so they release less energy by aerobic respiration and the smoker tires quickly.

questions.p:
Question 8
This question is about the Earth and space.
questions.q: (a) Which description of a galaxy is correct?
c: a huge group of stars and planetary systems, with dust and gas, held together by gravity
one star with the planets that orbit it
a cloud of gas around one planet
all the moons in the Solar System
questions.e: A **galaxy** contains billions of stars, many with planetary systems, plus clouds of dust and gas, all held together by gravity. B describes a planetary system, such as our Solar System. The answer is A.

questions.p:
Question 8
This question is about the Earth and space.
questions.q: (b) Which statement about asteroids is correct?
c: Asteroids are small stars that give out their own light.
Asteroids are rocks, smaller than planets, left over from when the planetary system formed.
Asteroids are clouds of gas between the planets.
Asteroids are bigger than planets and orbit the Moon.
questions.e: Asteroids are **rocks**, smaller than planets. They are pieces of rock **left over from the formation** of the Solar System that never joined together to make a planet. The answer is B.

questions.p:
Question 8
This question is about the Earth and space.
questions.q: (c) Which statement describes the **climate** of Aswan, not its weather?
c: It rained for ten minutes in Aswan yesterday.
Tomorrow the temperature in Aswan will be 41 °C.
There is a strong wind in Aswan this morning.
Aswan has very hot, dry summers and almost no rain in most years.
questions.e: **Weather** is the conditions on one day or over a few days. **Climate** is the usual (average) pattern of weather in a place over many years. Only D describes the pattern over many years. The answer is D.

questions.p:
Question 8
This question is about the Earth and space.
questions.q: (d) Scientists say that the Earth's climate has changed many times between ice ages and warm periods. Give **one** piece of evidence scientists use for this.
questions.ms: 1 mark for any one: ice cores (the air bubbles / layers trapped in ancient ice); fossils of plants or animals that lived in a different climate (e.g. tropical fossils in cold places); rocks and land shapes made by glaciers in places that are warm today; layers of sediment on the sea floor. Do not accept 'the weather changes every day'.
questions.e: For example, **ice cores**: deep ice in Antarctica contains tiny bubbles of air trapped hundreds of thousands of years ago, which show what the atmosphere and temperature were like. Fossils of animals or plants from a very different climate are also evidence.

questions.p:
Question 8
This question is about the Earth and space.
questions.q: (e) Name **one** gas in the atmosphere whose increase is making the Earth's climate warmer.
questions.e: **Carbon dioxide** (or methane). These greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere; more of them makes the Earth's average temperature rise.

questions.q: (e) Explain why door handles are fixed on the side of the door furthest from the hinges.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the distance from the pivot (hinges) is larger. 1 mark: so the same force gives a bigger moment (turning effect) / a smaller force is needed to open the door (moment = force × distance). Do not accept 'it is easier' with no reason.
questions.e: The hinges are the pivot. moment = force × distance, so the larger the distance from the hinges, the **bigger the moment** for the same force. With the handle far from the hinges, only a small force is needed to open the door.

questions.q: (b) Sprinters wear shoes with small metal spikes underneath. Why do the spikes help them to grip the track?
c: The spikes increase the area touching the track, so the pressure is smaller.
The spikes have a small area, so the pressure is large and they press into the track.
The spikes make the runner's weight smaller.
The spikes have a large area, so the pressure is large.
questions.e: The runner's weight acts on the tiny area of the spike tips. A small area gives a **large pressure**, so the spikes press into the track and grip it. The answer is B.

Question 3
This question is about pressure and particles on sports day.
questions.q: (c) A teacher pumps more air into a football. Use ideas about particles to explain why the pressure inside the ball increases.
questions.ms: 1 mark: there are more (air) particles inside the ball. 1 mark: so there are more collisions (of particles) with the inside wall of the ball each second / more force on the wall. Do not accept 'the particles get bigger' or 'the particles expand'.
questions.e: Gas pressure is caused by particles hitting the walls of the container. Pumping adds **more particles** to the same space, so there are **more collisions** with the inside of the ball every second, which push harder on it: the pressure goes up.

questions.q: (d) Spectators at the far end of the field can smell the food being grilled. Use ideas about particles to explain how the smell reaches them.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the particles (of the smell / gas) move randomly / constantly / in all directions. 1 mark: they spread out from where there are many (high concentration) to where there are few (low concentration) / they mix (intermingle) with the air particles. Accept 'diffusion' as part of the second mark only with the idea of spreading or mixing.
questions.e: This is **diffusion**. Particles of the smelly gas are always moving randomly. They collide with and mix with the air particles and spread out from where they are concentrated (near the grill) to where there are few of them, until some reach the spectators' noses.

questions.q: (c) Explain why the light changes direction when it goes from the air into the glass.
questions.ms: 1 mark: light slows down / changes speed when it enters the glass (glass is denser than air). Do not accept 'the glass reflects it'.
questions.e: Light travels more **slowly** in glass than in air. When a ray enters the glass at an angle, the change of speed makes it change direction: this is **refraction**.

questions.p:
Question 5
This question is about light and colour: a rainbow and the coloured lights on a school stage.
questions.q: (e) On the stage, a singer wears a white shirt and blue trousers. Only a red spotlight shines on him. Describe and explain what colour his shirt and his trousers look.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the shirt looks red because white reflects all colours, so it reflects the red light. 1 mark: the trousers look black because blue (objects) absorb red light / reflect only blue light, and there is no blue light to reflect. Colour without a reason gets no mark.
questions.e: A white object reflects every colour that falls on it, so the shirt reflects the red light and **looks red**. Blue trousers reflect only blue light and absorb the other colours. There is no blue in the red spotlight, so the red is absorbed, no light is reflected and the trousers **look black**.

Question 5
This question is about light and colour: a rainbow and the coloured lights on a school stage.
questions.q: (f) A spotlight beam hits a flat mirror on the stage. The angle of incidence is 25°. What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray?
questions.e: Law of reflection: angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 25°. Both angles are measured from the normal, on opposite sides, so the angle between the rays is 25° + 25° = **50°**.

Question 6
In the chemistry laboratory, Laila tests the colouring in an orange sports drink, S. She uses paper chromatography to compare it with four food dyes, P, Q, R and T.
questions.q: (c) Laila also makes some copper sulfate crystals. Her 20 g sample contains 18.4 g of copper sulfate. The rest is water and unreacted copper oxide. Calculate the percentage purity of Laila's copper sulfate. Show your working.
questions.e: percentage purity = mass of the pure substance ÷ total mass × 100 = 18.4 ÷ 20 × 100 = **92%**. (M1 for 18.4 ÷ 20 (× 100); A1 for 92.)

Question 6
In the chemistry laboratory, Laila tests the colouring in an orange sports drink, S. She uses paper chromatography to compare it with four food dyes, P, Q, R and T.
questions.q: (d) Laila's copper sulfate is not pure. Suggest **one** reason why the product of a chemical reaction is often not pure.
questions.ms: 1 mark for any one: some reactant is left over / unreacted (e.g. copper oxide); more than one product is made / other (side) reactions happen; the reactants were not pure; the product is mixed with the solvent (water) / dirt from the apparatus.
questions.e: For example, some of a reactant does not react and stays mixed with the product (like the unreacted copper oxide), or the reaction makes more than one product, so the product is an **impure mixture**.

(e) Laila makes two sugary sports drinks.

A | 30 | 500

Which drink, A or B, is more concentrated?
questions.e: Compare the mass in the same volume. A: 30 g in 500 cm³ = 6 g in 100 cm³. B: 20 g in 250 cm³ = 8 g in 100 cm³. **B** has more sugar particles in each cm³, so it is more concentrated.

questions.q: (f) The school nurse keeps instant cold packs for sports injuries. When a cold pack is squeezed, a solid dissolves in the water inside. The temperature falls from 21 °C to 4 °C. Is dissolving this solid exothermic or endothermic?
questions.e: The temperature **falls** (by 17 °C), so energy is taken in from the surroundings: the process is **endothermic**.

questions.q: (b) The climate goes through a cycle of ice ages and warm periods. How many thousand years are there between one warm period and the next?
questions.e: Warm peaks are at 400, 300, 200 and 100 thousand years ago (and today), so the cycle repeats every **100 thousand years** (100 000 years). Climate cycles take place over very long time periods.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read the worked solution and the mark scheme for **every** question, including the ones you got right.
For each written answer, compare your words with the mark scheme point by point. If your answer was only half right, write the full answer again in your notebook.

Make a list of the topic tags of the questions you lost marks on, then revisit those lessons. Biology: "Joints and Antagonistic Muscles", "Blood and Its Components", "Breathing, Gas Exchange and Diffusion in the Lungs", "A Balanced Diet, Energy Stores and Lifestyle", "Aerobic Respiration", "Ecosystems, Bioaccumulation and Invasive Species".

Chemistry: "The Structure of the Atom", "Purity, Concentration and Chromatography", "Word Equations, Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions", "The Reactivity of Metals", "Impure Products and Solubility of Salts".

Physics: "Speed and Distance–Time Graphs", "Balanced and Unbalanced Forces, and Moments", "Pressure, Particles and Diffusion", "Reflection and Refraction", "Dispersion and Colour", "Magnetic Fields and Electromagnets".

Earth and space: "The Earth's Magnetic Field and Earth's Resources", "Climate, Weather and Climate Change", "Galaxies and Asteroids". For the investigation questions (variables, anomalous results, means, risks, improvements), revisit "Thinking and Working Scientifically: Models, Investigations and Analysing Results".
Check your calculations: did you write the formula, show the working and give the unit? Many marks are lost on missing units.
A week later, try Practice Test 2 under timed conditions and compare your scores.
